prompt:
A simulated brick world had this hidden rule:
In this world the agent's observation shows the target shifted: the target, missing, extra and target-height channels are rolled 4 columns toward higher x, wrapping around. The world, its designs and scoring are as described.

Below is what an AI scientist wrote during a search in that world: its analysis at every round, in order, and the
name and hypothesis of the trial it ended with. Does the text, anywhere, state the rule?
- "yes": it states the rule's substance (what is changed and how).
- "partly": it identifies the right kind of change but not its specifics.
- "no": anything else.

## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no trials yet. The starting architecture scored 0.000 on both seeds, so it never learned to make an exact build within the budget. That leaves two likely causes: too few samples or updates, or a weak prior about where a brick lands. The task depends on layers. A brick's landing layer is the maximum height under its footprint. A good move fills missing target cells at that layer and does not cover missing cells below it. Any tiling counts, because success is judged cell by cell, so good decisions are mostly local to the footprint and the layer. The baseline flattens all layers into channels at the start, so it has to rebuild this from mixed features. I propose a 2x2 design. One candidate keeps the baseline network and changes only the recipe: fewer PPO epochs, so more samples, and a higher lr. Two candidates use a new layer-wise footprint scorer, once with the default recipe and once with the new recipe. Since 0 vs 0 is uninformative, any nonzero result is a signal.

### Round 2
All six training runs scored exactly 0. That covers the baseline and the layer-wise scorer, each with the default recipe and with the 2-epoch, more-samples recipe. Training success was also 0, so the agents never built a design exactly, not even on the training stream. Extra samples did not help, and neither did a strong per-layer prior that assumes the stated layer order and anchor position. Three explanations are still open. (1) Too few policy updates: the default runs make only 32 PPO updates, and the short discount gives little credit for finishing a build. (2) The world may differ from the description, for example in action indexing or anchor alignment, which would break heads that assume the top-left anchor. The note warns about this, and a network with only 1x1 layers, like r1c2, cannot adapt to it. (3) Too little receptive field or depth. This round tests each one: a recipe with many small updates on the unchanged baseline, a deeper residual trunk plus a 3x3 per-type head that does not assume the anchor position, and a dense head that makes no alignment assumption at all.

### Round 3
All 6 trials scored exactly 0 on dev, and also 0 on training success over the last 10% of training. These included recipe changes (more samples, more updates, longer horizon), deeper trunks, a per-layer scorer and a dense head. The baseline head should be able to represent a decent greedy bottom-up policy, so a total failure even on training designs suggests one of two things. Either the world departs from the description in a way that breaks the conv logit alignment (for example a transposed or flipped action index, swapped footprints or a moved DONE index), or learning is far too slow. Seed noise does not matter while everything is 0. Any nonzero score wins, so this round hedges. Candidate 1 is a head that can learn flips, transposes, type swaps, anchor shifts and per-action biases. Candidate 2 is a fully alignment-free dense policy. Candidate 3 is the baseline with the most samples the budget allows. All three feed the legality mask in as input, because it reveals the true action geometry.

### Round 4
Nine trials covering two recipes, two inductive biases (a layer-wise scorer and a deep trunk), two hedges against action misalignment (a dihedral head and a dense MLP) and up to 400k steps all scored exactly 0. Training success in the last 10% was also 0 every time. Seed noise cannot explain that, and neither can a single wrong architecture choice. My best guess is that the agent learns to press DONE immediately. Early random placements earn negative reward, while DONE gives 0 and is always legal. DONE then has a consistently positive advantage, about 0 minus V(s). That advantage grows with gamma, and earlier trials raised gamma to 0.97. A state-independent DONE bias learns much faster than per-cell placement skill. After the collapse, episodes return 0 and the agent never succeeds, which matches what we see. For this last round, all three candidates use the same counter to that collapse: lower gamma and lambda, more entropy bonus, and a DONE logit that starts at zero with a fixed offset of minus 2. I apply it to three different networks (baseline, layer-wise scorer, deep trunk) to maximise the chance that at least one scores above 0.

## Trial it ended with
name: Deep trunk + mask + anti-collapse
hypothesis: A residual trunk of four 3x3 convs (9x9 receptive field), the legality mask as input, and a 3x3 local logit head that can learn anchor shifts. Recipe: 3 epochs, gamma 0.9, lambda 0.85, entropy 0.02, and a DONE head that starts at zero with an offset of minus 2. This tests the anti-collapse idea on a network with more context and the misalignment hedges. Refuted if it stays at 0 while the other anti-collapse candidates score.

Return a JSON object: "verdict" ("yes", "partly" or "no") and "evidence" (at most 80 words, quoting the text and
naming the round it comes from).

reply.evidence: The text never says the observed target channels are shifted. Round 2 suggests "the world may differ... in action indexing or anchor alignment", and Round 3 lists "a transposed or flipped action index, swapped footprints or a moved DONE index". Both are guesses about action-space misalignment, not about the target being rolled 4 columns relative to the height map. Round 4 then settles on an immediate-DONE collapse as the explanation, and the final trial's 3x3 head could not cover a 4-column shift anyway.
